pass_a_gloss: [...] stones of the altars cut down like fine dust, and their trees will not remain, and their idols cut out like a forest far off. Having rubbed in through the middle the reproof against those who had acted impiously toward the holy prophets, the blessed prophet holds again to the sequence of the thoughts, and says as from the person of God: Because of this the lawlessness of Jacob will be taken away. Because of this: what sort? For since he will not be slain as he himself slew, nor yet will he be struck as he himself struck, the calmness that is in God always conquering the human pettinesses, and not in every way and wholly bringing on penalties equally matched to the offences of those on earth, but rather mixing the wrath with gentleness. For this reason he says: The lawlessness of Jacob will be taken away, that is, he will obtain loving-kindness, and he will remit to him in due times the charges, he will free him even from the accusations themselves; and this is his blessing. For he promised to Abraham, saying: Truly I will bless you, and multiplying I will multiply your seed. But the divine Abraham would not truly have been blessed, nor would his seed have been multiplied, those from his blood being required to pay penalties proportional to the sins. But since, although having done nothing of the good things, and rather having been carried down toward the last unholiness, they too have been enriched with the forgiveness, the ground of the blessing has been kept and has passed through to them. When then I take away, he says, his sin, this will be the manner of the blessing for him. And he makes clear the time at which he too will be free of the offences. For when, he says, those called through the faith to knowledge of the God who truly is will make war against the ancient error, when altars and precincts and the swarm of idols come out of the middle, when they consume with fire the temples laboured on for the lifeless idols; when they cut out their trees and besides these the handmade things, like some forest; then indeed then God will remit also to those from Israel themselves the stumblings. And this, I think, is what the divine Paul said [light]: But when the fullness of the nations comes in, then all Israel will be saved. For wholly to burn down temples, and to shear off the groves planted beside them, and to add also the overthrow of the statues themselves, would signify nothing else than that surely, that of those of old who strayed and worshipped the works of their own hands there will be a change toward knowledge of truth, so that they come to this [degree] of love of God as also to lay hands on the things of old worshipped by them, and those of w[ood] [the section breaks off].
pass_b_english: “… stones of the altars broken to pieces like fine dust; and their trees will not remain, and their idols cut down like a forest far off” (Isaiah 27:9).

Having set in between his reproof of those who had acted impiously toward the holy prophets, the blessed prophet again holds to the sequence of his thoughts, and says, as from the person of God: “Therefore the lawlessness of Jacob will be taken away” (Isaiah 27:9). “Therefore”: for what reason? Because he will not be slain as he himself slew, nor struck as he himself struck (Isaiah 27:7). For the gentleness that is in God always overcomes human pettiness; he does not in every way and in every case bring penalties equal to the offenses committed on earth, but rather tempers his wrath with mildness.

This is why he says: “The lawlessness of Jacob will be taken away”; that is, he will receive loving-kindness, and God will in due time remit his charges and free him even from the accusations themselves. “And this is his blessing.” For God promised Abraham, saying: “Surely I will bless you, and I will greatly multiply your seed” (Genesis 22:17). But the godlike Abraham would not truly have been blessed, nor would his seed have been multiplied, if those of his blood had been required to pay penalties in proportion to their sins. But since they too, though they had done nothing good, and had rather been carried down into the utmost impiety, were enriched with forgiveness, the ground of the blessing has been kept and has passed on to them. “When, therefore, I take away his sin,” he says, “this will be the manner of his blessing.”

He also makes plain the time at which Jacob too will be free of his offenses. For when, he says, those called through faith to the knowledge of him who is truly God take the field against the ancient error; when altars and sacred precincts and the swarm of idols are taken out of the way; when they consume with fire the temples built with toil for lifeless idols; when they cut down their trees, and besides these the things made with hands, like a forest: then, then indeed God will remit their stumblings to those of Israel as well. And this, I think, is what the godlike Paul declared: “But when the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, then all Israel will be saved” (Romans 11:25–26).

For to burn the temples down completely, to shear off the groves planted beside them, and to add as well the overthrow of the statues themselves, would signify nothing else, surely, than this: that those who long wandered in error and worshipped the works of their own hands will be changed and come to the knowledge of the truth, and will reach such love of God as even to lay hands on the things they once worshipped, and those of …

choices.why: Cyril answers Isaiah 27:7 here; the contrast is God's mildness, not human judgment.
rejected: an invented contrast with human judgment

choices.why: The calm of God that overcomes human pettiness.
If penalties had matched the sins, Abraham's seed would not have been multiplied.
φῶς after ἔφησε appears to be a printing slip and is not translated.
